hints: Remember what proton number tells you from the Periodic Table and how it is different from nucleon number for Mg and Al.
Think about how forming a 2+ or 3+ ion changes the electron count compared with the neutral atom, while protons stay unchanged.
walkthrough:
Sort out protons from nucleons**
Proton number is just the atomic number. Magnesium is 12 and aluminium is 13, so those numbers never change when an ion forms. Nucleon number is already given as 24 and 27, that is protons plus neutrons.

Count electrons after losing charge**
A neutral Mg atom has 12 electrons, but $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has lost 2, leaving $12 - 2 = 10$. A neutral Al atom has 13 electrons, but $\text{Al}^{3+}$ has lost 3, leaving $13 - 3 = 10$. Both ions end up with 10 electrons, isoelectronic with neon.

Final answer: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$: nucleon number 24, proton number 12, electrons 10
$\text{Al}^{3+}$: nucleon number 27, proton number 13, electrons 10

hints: Compare the electron arrangements of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and decide if shielding by inner shells is different.
Compare the number of protons pulling on that same arrangement of electrons in each ion.
Link a stronger pull per electron to what happens to the radius of the electron cloud.
walkthrough:
See that both ions look the same electronically**
Both $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ have 10 electrons in the arrangement 2,8. That means the inner shielding is essentially identical, the same shells screening the nucleus.

Spot the only difference, the nucleus**
Aluminium has 13 protons while magnesium has 12. So the same 10 electrons in $\text{Al}^{3+}$ feel the pull of one extra proton with no extra shielding to cancel it.

Pull the cloud in tighter**
Greater effective nuclear attraction drags the electron cloud closer to the nucleus. That is why $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is the smaller ion.

Final answer: $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is smaller than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.
Both ions have the same electron arrangement with the same shielding.
$\text{Al}^{3+}$ has greater nuclear charge (13 protons vs 12 protons) so greater attraction for the remaining electrons, pulling them closer.

hints: Picture what sodium metal looks like at the particle level, a regular lattice of one type of particle surrounded by mobile charge.
walkthrough:
Draw the metallic model**
Show a neat grid of at least four touching circles in rows, each labelled $\text{Na}^{+}$ or + for the positive ion. Then dot or shade the space around them and label it as delocalised electrons or sea of electrons. The regular lattice plus labelled mobile electrons earns the mark.
Final answer: Regular arrangement of at least 2 x 2 $\text{Na}^{+}$ ions (circles labelled + or $\text{Na}^{+}$) surrounded by sea of delocalised electrons (labelled).

hints: Think about what type of lattice silicon forms and what must be broken to allow atoms to move as a liquid.
walkthrough:
Link high melting point to strong network**
Silicon is not made of separate molecules. Every Si atom is covalently bonded tetrahedrally into a giant 3D network. Melting means breaking those strong $\text{Si-Si}$ covalent bonds throughout the lattice, which needs a huge input of thermal energy, so the melting point is very high.
Final answer: Si has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds that require a large amount of energy to break.

hints: Recall whether P, S and Cl are giant or simple molecular, and how their melting points compare with giant structures like Mg.
Think about the order of melting points for simple molecules from $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to $\text{P}_{4}$ to $\text{S}_{8}$ and what controls it.
walkthrough:
Drop well below magnesium**
P, S and Cl exist as simple molecules ($\text{P}_{4}$, $\text{S}_{8}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}$). Melting only overcomes weak London dispersion forces between molecules, not strong metallic or covalent bonds, so all three points sit much lower on the graph than Mg.

Order the three molecules**
Larger molecules have more electrons and stronger temporary dipoles. $\text{S}_{8}$ is largest so it has the highest melting point of the three, then $\text{P}_{4}$, then $\text{Cl}_{2}$ lowest. Draw low points rising from Cl up to P up to S.

Final answer: All three melting points plotted lower than Mg.
Trend shown as Cl < P < S (S highest of the three, Cl lowest).

hints: Think about the oxide formed in excess oxygen for Na and for S, and whether each oxide is ionic and solid or molecular and gaseous.
Recall what pH results when a Group 1 oxide dissolves compared with a non-metal oxide that forms a strong acid.
walkthrough:
Work out the state**
Sodium forms ionic $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$, a solid at room temperature. Sulfur in excess oxygen forms molecular $\text{SO}_{2}$ or $\text{SO}_{3}$, which are gases at room temperature.

Predict the solution pH**
$\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$ reacts to give $\text{NaOH}$, a strong alkali, so pH about 13, in the 10-14 range. Sulfur oxides give sulfurous or sulfuric acid, strongly acidic, so pH about 1-2, in the 0-4 range.

Final answer: Na oxide: solid, pH 10-14 (approx 13)
S oxide: gas, pH 0-4 (approx 1-2)

hints: Consider what happens when an alkaline solution and an acidic solution are mixed together.
walkthrough:
Name the clash of opposites**
You are mixing the strongly alkaline sodium hydroxide solution with the strongly acidic sulfur oxide solution. $\text{H}^{+}$ from the acid joins $\text{OH}^{-}$ from the alkali to make water. That is the classic acid-base or neutralisation reaction.
Final answer: Acid-base (neutralisation) reaction.

hints: Remember that $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ is an acidic oxide that reacts fully with excess water to give phosphoric acid.
walkthrough:
Build the hydrolysis equation**
Phosphorus(V) oxide pulls water in to make $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$. One $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ unit needs 6 $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to supply enough H and O for 4 $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ molecules: $$\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$$

hints: Think about the two opposite chemical characters a substance like $\text{Al(OH)}_{3}$ can show.
walkthrough:
Define two-way character**
Amphoteric simply means it can act two ways. $\text{Al(OH)}_{3}$ can behave as a base and neutralise acids, and it can also behave as an acid and react with alkalis. That dual reactivity is the definition.
Final answer: Reacts with both acids and bases (shows both acidic and basic behaviour).

hints: Think about the complex ion formed when $\text{Al(OH)}_{3}$ accepts an $\text{OH}^{-}$ from $\text{NaOH}$.
walkthrough:
Show the alkali dissolving the hydroxide**
Here $\text{Al(OH)}_{3}$ acts as an acid toward $\text{NaOH}$. It accepts one more $\text{OH}^{-}$ to form the soluble tetrahydroxoaluminate ion: $$\text{Al(OH)}_{3} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaAl(OH)}_{4}$$ The white solid dissolves to give a colourless solution.
